title: मैंने खाना खाया — the subject that changes its ending
title_target: कल आपने क्या किया? — kal aapne kyaa kiyaa?
goal: Tackle the most unfamiliar part of Hindi for English speakers: in a past sentence with an object, the subject takes the ending ने — and the verb stops agreeing with the subject and starts agreeing with the object.
bekal: recognizing when ने is used and when it isn't
using मैंने, आपने, उसने, हमने, उन्होंने
making the verb agree with its object
recognizing verbs that never take ने

dialogs.title: संवाद — Why "aap" becomes "aapne"
dialogs.intro: This is the hardest unit in the book, and the dialogue is deliberately written like a lesson — because that's how a real Ani would ask about it. Read it slowly, and don't worry if it takes two sittings.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: "Where did you go yesterday" — there it's "aap". "What did you do yesterday" — here it's "aapne".
lines.literal: yesterday — you — where — went — there — "you". yesterday — you-NE — what — done — here — "you-NE".

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: why? both — gone-by(obl.) — kal — of(fem.) — matter — are.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: "Jana" has no object. "Karna" has an object — "what".
lines.literal: "go" — of — any — object — not. "do" — of — object — is — "what".

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Exactly! And look — "khana" is masculine, so it's "khaya".
lines.literal: exactly! and — look — "food" — masculine — is, therefore — "eaten(masc.)".

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Because "chai" is feminine. The verb goes along with the object.
lines.literal: because — "tea" — feminine — is. verb — object — of — with — goes(fem.) — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: With the object? Not with the subject?
lines.literal: object — of — with? subject — of — with — not?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Yes. This is the hardest part of all.
lines.literal: yes. this-very — of-all — hard — thing — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Now I see why Hindi is hard!
lines.literal: now — understanding — came — that — Hindi — why — hard — is!

notes: **The rule has two conditions, and both must hold at once.** Condition one: the sentence is in the **past**. Condition two: the verb has an **object**. If both are true, the subject takes **ने**. If either one fails, there's no ने at all. ⚠️ That's why it's *मैं गई* (go — no object) but *मैंने खाना खाया* (eat — with an object).

**And as soon as ने appears, the verb stops agreeing with the subject.** It starts agreeing with the **object**. *मैंने खाना खाया* — खाया is masculine because **खाना** is masculine, not because of the speaker. *मैंने चाय पी* — पी is feminine because **चाय** is feminine. A man and a woman say both sentences **exactly the same way**. ⚠️ This is the complete reverse of the Unit 4 rule, and that's where all the difficulty lies.
**If the object is plural, the verb is plural.** *मैंने किताबें पढ़ीं* (किताबें feminine plural → पढ़ीं), *मैंने आम खाए* (आम masculine plural → खाए). Again, the subject has no influence at all.

**One very useful way out: if the object takes को, the verb goes neutral -आ.** *मैंने उसको देखा* (I saw him/her), *मैंने बच्चों को बुलाया* (I called the children). The neutral form is always **-आ**, whatever the gender and number. Since **people** as objects almost always take को, sentences about people are much easier than sentences about things.

**The subject forms: मैंने, तूने, तुमने, आपने, इसने, उसने, हमने, इन्होंने, उन्होंने.** ⚠️ Watch the last two — **इन्होंने** and **उन्होंने** — not *इनने*/*उनने*. They're irregular and must be learned as they are; both are very common, because respected people always take the plural form.

**A few verbs with objects still DON'T take ने, and these must be memorized.** **लाना** (bring), **भूलना** (forget), **मिलना** (meet), and **बोलना** in everyday use. So *मैं किताब लाई* (not *मैंने*), *मैं भूल गई* (not *मैंने*). There are only a few, but all four come up often.

**How much does it matter if you get it wrong?** Honestly: not much. Indians will still understand *मैं खाना खाया*, just as English speakers understand a foreigner's broken grammar. But ने is **the marker that most quickly shows someone has really mastered Hindi** — more than vocabulary, more than pronunciation. So do the exercises seriously, and give yourself weeks, not days.

grammars.title: When ने, when not
after: ⚠️ With names and ordinary nouns, **ने stands as a separate word** after them: *राम ने*, *मेरी बहन ने*, *बच्चों ने*. Notice that the noun goes into the oblique form, because ने is a postposition like the others.

grammars.title: The most common verbs with objects
after: ⚠️ **पीना → पी**, **लेना → लिया / ली** and **देना → दिया / दी** are frequent irregular forms. Learn these three now; the rest follow the regular pattern.

blocks.text: A story about yesterday almost always mixes two kinds of sentences: those with an object (with ने) and those without (no ने). Watch the switching in the example below, and read it aloud until the switching feels natural.

head: हिंदी
Pronunciation
Meaning
ने?
rows: Then I went to the market.
In the afternoon I watched a film.
रात को मैं जल्दी सो गई।
raat ko maiⁿ jal-dii so ga-ii
At night I went to bed early.

blocks.title: A way to practice that really works
items: **Write five sentences about your day every evening** — three with an object, two without. Five sentences, not fifty. What works isn't the number but the switching.
**Before you write, ask one thing: what's the object?** If you can name the thing, use ने and check that thing's gender. If there's no thing, don't use ने.
**Start with people as objects.** *मैंने उनको देखा*, *मैंने माँ को फ़ोन किया* — they all take को, so the verb is neutral -आ and you don't have to think about gender at all. It's the easiest way in.
⚠️ **Don't wait until you're fluent to start speaking.** A wrong ने sentence is still far more useful than a sentence never spoken.

blocks.text: One note that may be comforting. This ने pattern has a name in linguistics — **ergative** — and it isn't just a Hindi quirk: Georgian, Basque, Kurdish and a number of languages in Papua use it too. Hindi inherited it from the way Sanskrit formed passive sentences: *मैंने खाना खाया* once meant roughly "the food was eaten by me". If you read it that way — **the object is the center of the sentence, the subject is just a detail** — the whole rule suddenly makes sense, including why the verb agrees with the object. Many learners say this is the explanation that finally made it click.

vocab.en: subject marker in past sentences with an object

exercises.prompt: Decide: ने or not? Write the subject form.
Put the words in the right order.
Translate into Hindi. Assume you are a woman.
items: I had breakfast, then I went to the market.
In the afternoon I watched a film.
At night I went to bed early.

answers: मैं — मैंने — उसने — वे — आपने — मैं
कल आपने क्या किया? — मैंने खाना खाया। — मैंने चाय पी। — शाम को हमने फ़िल्म देखी। — मैंने बाज़ार से सब्ज़ी ख़रीदी।
कल आपने क्या किया? — मैंने नाश्ता किया, फिर मैं बाज़ार गई। — मैंने सब्ज़ी ख़रीदी। — मैंने खाना बनाया। — शाम को मैंने फ़िल्म देखी। — रात को मैं जल्दी सो गई।
